questions.q: What must a person who makes a vow not do?
questions.a: He must not break his promise.

questions.q: If a young woman who lives in her father’s house makes a vow to Yahweh and her father hears her vow but says nothing to reverse the vow, is the vow in force?
If a young woman who lives in her father’s house makes a vow to Yahweh and her father stops her on the day that he hears of it, is the vow in force?
questions.a: No, the vow is not in force.

questions.q: If a young woman who is married makes her vows and her husband hears about it and does nothing to stop her, are the vows in force?
questions.a: Yes, the vows are in force.

questions.q: If a young woman’s husband stops her on the day that he hears about her vows, are the vows in force?
questions.a: No, the vows are not in force.

questions.q: If a widow or a divorced woman makes a vow to Yahweh, is the vow in force?
questions.a: Yes, the vow is in force.

questions.q: If a married woman makes a vow while living in her husband’s household and her husband hears about it but says nothing, does her vow remain in force?
questions.a: Yes, her vow must remain in force.

questions.q: If a married woman makes a vow while living in her husband’s household and her husband cancels it on the day that he hears about it, is the vow in force?
questions.a: No, her vow will not remain in force.

questions.q: If a married woman makes a vow while living in her husband’s household and her husband cancels it on the day that he hears about it, is the vow in force?
questions.a: No, her vow will not remain in force.

questions.q: If a married woman makes a vow while living in her husband’s household and her husband hears of it and says nothing to her, is the vow in force?
questions.a: Yes, her vows must remain in force.

questions.q: If a wife’s husband tries to cancel her vow a long time after he has heard about it, is the vow in force?
questions.a: Yes, it will be in force, and if he breaks it, he will be responsible for her sin and suffer the penalty for breaking it.
They concerned vows between a husband and his wife, and between a father and his young unmarried daughter who still lived in his house.

commentary.text: The cases wherein vows might be released.

Verses 1, 2 No man can be bound by his own promise to do what he is already, by the Divine precept, forbidden to do. In other matters the command is, that he shall not break his words, through he may change his mind.

Two cases of vows are determined. The case of a daughter in her father's house. When her vow comes to his knowledge, it is in his power either to confirm it or do it away. The law is plain in the case of a wife. If her husband allows her vow, though only by silence, it stands. If he disallows it, her obligation to her husband takes place of it; for to him she ought to be in subjection, as unto the Lord. The Divine law consults the good order of families. It is fit that every man should bear rule in his own house, and have his wife and children in subjection; rather than that this great rule should be broken, or any encouragement be given to inferior relations to break those bonds asunder, God releases the obligation even of a solemn vow. So much does religion secure the welfare of all societies; and in it the families of the earth have a blessing.
